title: Chunk a Document for Retrieval
statement:
A knowledge base answers questions by searching small pieces of each document, not whole files. Before you embed a document you cut it into chunks. Good chunks end at sentence boundaries, never exceed the size limit, and repeat a few words from the previous chunk so a fact split across the cut can still be found.

Write def solution(text, max_words, overlap) that returns the list of chunk strings.

Words and sentences. Words are the pieces of text.split() (any run of whitespace separates words). A sentence ends at a word whose last character is ., ? or !; the mark stays on the word. Any words left after the last mark form a final sentence.

Packing. Build one chunk at a time as a list of words. A chunk's words are its overlap words (copied from the previous chunk) followed by its new words. To close a chunk: output its words joined by single spaces, then start the next chunk with the last overlap words of the one you closed (no words if overlap is 0). For each sentence, in order:

  1. If the sentence does not fit (current words + sentence words > max_words) and the chunk has at least one new word, close the chunk.
  2. Then, if the sentence fits, add all of its words.
  3. Otherwise the sentence is too long even for a fresh chunk: add its words one at a time, closing the chunk each time it already holds max_words words before adding the next word.

At the end, close the last chunk only if it has at least one new word. Empty or all-whitespace text returns [].

examples.input: text = "Rates rose in May. Fees are waived for seniors. Apply online.", max_words = 6, overlap = 2
examples.output: ["Rates rose in May.", "in May. Fees are waived for", "waived for seniors. Apply online."]
examples.why: Sentence 2 does not fit after sentence 1, so chunk 1 closes. Chunk 2 starts with "in May." and sentence 2 still does not fit, so it is split by words at 6. Chunk 3 starts with "waived for" and takes the rest.

examples.input: text = "One two. Three four. Five six.", max_words = 4, overlap = 0
examples.why: Two 2-word sentences fill a 4-word chunk exactly. With no overlap the next chunk starts empty.

examples.input: text = "Short. This sentence has far too many words", max_words = 3, overlap = 1
examples.output: ["Short.", "Short. This sentence", "sentence has far", "far too many", "many words"]
examples.why: The second sentence has 7 words and no end mark. It cannot fit in any chunk, so it is cut by words; each chunk after the first starts with the last word of the previous one.

constraints: words contain no whitespace; an end mark only counts as the last character of a word (so 3.14 or e.g., do not end a sentence, but e.g. does)

think.q: What are the three things that can happen to a sentence?
think.a: It fits in the current chunk and is added. It does not fit, so the chunk closes and the sentence starts the next one (after the overlap words). Or it is longer than any chunk can hold, so it is cut by words.

Sentences: [A b.] [C d e.] [F.]. Chunk 1 takes "A b." (2 words); "C d e." would make 5, so close "A b.". Chunk 2 starts with overlap "b." then "C d e." = 4 words. "F." would make 5: close. Chunk 3 = "e. F.". Result ["A b.", "b. C d e.", "e. F."].

think.q: What is the obvious shortcut, and why is it wrong?
think.a: Cut every max_words words. It is one line, but it splits sentences in half and has no overlap. Retrieval quality drops because each chunk loses context. The brute force here keeps the chunk as a string and re-splits it to count words, which is correct but O(n × max_words).
"split into sentences", "pack", "at most" → string parsing plus greedy packing. Keep the current chunk as a list of words and a counter of how many are new; never re-split strings you built.

1. Split into sentences (lists of words).
  2. Keep cur (words) and fresh (new words in it).
  3. Write flush(): append " ".join(cur), keep the last overlap words, set fresh = 0.
  4. Per sentence: flush if it does not fit and fresh > 0; add it whole if it now fits; else add word by word, flushing when cur is full.
  5. Flush at the end if fresh > 0.

overlap = 0: cur[-0:] returns the whole list, an infinite-growth bug. Empty text. No punctuation at all. A sentence exactly max_words long. One sentence longer than max_words. Newlines and double spaces. A last chunk that would be only overlap (must not be emitted).

hints: Work with lists of words, not strings. text.split() with no argument already handles newlines and repeated spaces; a word ends a sentence if word.endswith((".", "?", "!")).
Track two numbers: len(cur) (for the size limit) and fresh, the count of words that are not overlap. "Close only if fresh > 0" stops you emitting a chunk that just repeats the previous one.
To keep the last k words use cur[len(cur) - k:]. Do not use cur[-k:]: when k is 0 it returns the whole list.
solution:
END_MARKS = ('.', '?', '!')

def split_sentences(text):
    # A sentence ends at a word whose last character is . ? or !
    sentences, current = [], []
    for word in text.split():
        current.append(word)
        if word.endswith(END_MARKS):
            sentences.append(current)
            current = []
    if current:                      # trailing words with no end mark
        sentences.append(current)
    return sentences

def solution(text, max_words, overlap):
    chunks = []
    cur = []        # words in the chunk being built
    fresh = 0       # how many of them are new (not copied overlap)

    def flush():
        nonlocal cur, fresh
        chunks.append(' '.join(cur))
        # careful: cur[-0:] is the WHOLE list, so slice from the front
        cur = cur[len(cur) - overlap:]
        fresh = 0

    for sentence in split_sentences(text):
        # Rule 2: close the chunk if the sentence does not fit and the chunk has new words
        if len(cur) + len(sentence) > max_words and fresh > 0:
            flush()
        if len(cur) + len(sentence) <= max_words:
            cur.extend(sentence)                 # Rule 1: whole sentence fits
            fresh += len(sentence)
        else:
            for word in sentence:                # Rule 3: too long, split by words
                if len(cur) == max_words:
                    flush()
                cur.append(word)
                fresh += 1
    if fresh > 0:                                # Rule 4: last chunk, unless it is only overlap
        chunks.append(' '.join(cur))
    return chunks
explain:
The solution is a greedy packer with one subtle state variable, fresh. Walk example 1 (max_words = 6, overlap = 2):

  • Sentences: "Rates rose in May." (4), "Fees are waived for seniors." (5), "Apply online." (2).
  • Chunk 1 takes sentence 1 (4 words). Sentence 2 would make 9 > 6, and the chunk has new words, so close it.
  • Chunk 2 starts with the overlap "in May." (2) + sentence 2 (5) = 7 > 6: still too long, so rule 3 adds words one at a time and closes at 6 words: "in May. Fees are waived for".
  • Chunk 3 starts with overlap "waived for", adds "seniors." (3 words); "Apply online." makes 5 ≤ 6, so it joins. End: close it.

Talk about the trade-off out loud: a larger overlap helps recall but stores and embeds more duplicate text. Then test overlap = 0 first, because that is where the [-0:] bug hides.
complexity: O(total words + total output words) time: each word is copied into at most a few chunks
